idiom_name: exhaustive pattern match over a sealed message ADT (or Akka Streams Partition)
implementation_notes: Scala's pattern matching turns the router into a total function over a closed algebraic data type: a sealed trait with one case class per message kind plus a match naming each destination replaces the router class, and the compiler warns when the match stops being exhaustive (a build error under -Xfatal-warnings), so a new message kind cannot silently route nowhere. When rules are value-based rather than type-based, a List[PartialFunction[Message, Destination]] composed with orElse is the rules-as-data form, with isDefinedAt as the guard; an unmatched value raises MatchError, so the fallback must be an explicit case. In an actor system the same ADT is the protocol and the match selects the target ActorRef, while a stream topology can use the library's Partition operator instead.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Message
final case class OrderCreated(order: Order) extends Message
final case class InvoiceIssued(invoice: Invoice) extends Message

def route(m: Message): Destination = m match {
  case OrderCreated(_)  => Orders        // exhaustive: no wildcard needed
  case InvoiceIssued(_) => Invoices
}
pitfalls: Only sealed hierarchies are checked: matching on a String discriminator compiles without a default and throws MatchError at runtime for an unhandled value.
Exhaustiveness is a warning, not an error, unless -Xfatal-warnings (or the stricter Scala 3 checks) is enabled - the guarantee is a build-flag decision.
PartialFunctions composed with orElse silently widen the accepted set: a rule added for one flow changes the behaviour of every router built from the same list.

variants.name: Akka Streams Partition (partitioner function)
variants.implementation_notes: The library form pushes the routing rule into the stream graph: Partition(n, partitioner) fans one stream out to n outlets, and each upstream element is emitted to exactly one of them according to the partitioner function applied to the element (verified in the Akka Streams reference), so the routing table is a function and the destinations are typed outlets with Reactive Streams back-pressure negotiated between them. Choose it when the destinations are stages of one pipeline and back-pressure should couple them; choose the pattern-match router when the destinations are independent channels or actors where one slow consumer must not hold back the others.
pitfalls: The outlet count is fixed when the graph is built, so a new destination means a new graph - runtime rule tables and stream partitions do not mix.
A partitioner that throws, or returns an index outside the outlet range, fails the stream: a routing mistake becomes an infrastructure incident rather than a misrouted message.
Back-pressure couples the routes: a stalled destination holds back the shared upstream, which is exactly the coupling an independent-destination router avoids.
